references.topic: Contractual standard of care: skill and care ordinarily provided by architects in the same or similar locality and circumstances.
references.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of B101-2017; confirm in your copy.

references.topic: Architect not required to execute certificates or consents requiring knowledge or services beyond the scope of the agreement.
Architect has no responsibility for discovery, presence, handling, removal or disposal of hazardous materials at the site.
Owner furnishes program, budget, surveys, geotechnical services, tests and reports; architect may rely on owner-furnished information.
Services required by unforeseen conditions or changes are additional services, some requiring owner's prior written authorization.

references.citation: 2024 AIA Code of Ethics: Rule 2.401; Canon VI, E.S. 6.5 (Climate Change), Rule 6.501
references.topic: Members must make reasonable efforts to inform clients of potential environmental impacts (2.401) and consider with clients the environmental effects of project decisions (6.501). E.S. 6.5 asks members to incorporate adaptation strategies for extreme weather.

references.citation: NCARB Model Rules of Conduct (rev. July 2023), Rules 1.1–1.3
references.topic: Primary duty is to protect public health, safety and welfare; act with reasonable care and competence, applying the knowledge and skill ordinarily applied by architects in good standing in the same locality (NCARB notes this rests on the common-law standard of care); don't knowingly design in violation of building laws.

questions.stem:
Five years after completion, a former client sues an architect after a visitor falls on a monumental stair, alleging negligent design. The architect's attorney points out that the stair met the building code in effect at the time and passed the building official's review. The client's attorney argues that the design still fell below professional standards.

How is the standard of care most often established in such a case?

options.text: By the building code in effect at the time of design
options.explanation: Code compliance is evidence, but codes are minimums, and the professional standard is broader.

options.text: By expert testimony from other architects
options.explanation: Correct. Experts testify to what a reasonably prudent architect would have done in similar circumstances.

options.text: By the language of the owner–architect agreement
options.explanation: The agreement states the general standard. Experts show what it required in the specific circumstances.

options.text: By the building official's approval of the permit
options.explanation: Plan approval doesn't establish that the design met the professional standard.

questions.explanation: Standard of care = ordinary, reasonable professional care, usually shown through expert testimony.

questions.stem:
An institutional owner sends a firm its standard agreement for a research building. One clause states that the architect 'shall perform all services to the highest professional standards and guarantees the documents will be free of errors and omissions.' The owner's representative calls it non-negotiable boilerplate that 'every architect signs.'

What is the primary concern with this clause?

options.text: It's an express warranty that may be uninsurable.
options.explanation: Correct. 'Highest standards' and 'guarantees' raise the duty above negligence, which professional liability policies generally exclude.

options.text: It matches the standard of care stated in B101-2017.
options.explanation: B101-2017 uses an ordinary skill-and-care standard.

options.text: It increases only the owner's obligations.
options.explanation: The clause binds the architect.

options.text: It's unenforceable and can be accepted safely.
options.explanation: Courts may enforce express promises. Never assume an onerous clause is harmless.

questions.explanation: Avoid warranty language (guarantee, ensure, highest, certify). Keep the ordinary standard of care.

questions.stem:
During construction of a two-story office building, the contractor discovers that the documents omitted code-required roof-access ladders and a roof hatch. The contractor prices the work as a change order, and the owner asks the architect to pay for it.

| Cost item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Ladders and hatch, if in the original bid | $6,000 |
| Ladders and hatch, priced now | $7,500 |
| Cutting and patching the completed roof deck | $1,500 |

Under the concept of betterment, what is the architect's likely responsibility?

options.explanation: This counts only the patching and misses the premium for buying the items late.
Correct. The owner pays the $6,000 it would have paid anyway. The architect may owe the added cost: $9,000 − $6,000.
That's the change-order price for the items, which includes the betterment the owner would have paid.
Charging the full cost would give the owner a windfall of $6,000.

questions.explanation:
1. Total cost now = $7,500 + $1,500 = $9,000
2. Owner's original cost (betterment) = $6,000
3. Added cost caused by the omission = $9,000 − $6,000 = $3,000

questions.stem:
An architect is documenting existing conditions for the renovation of a 1962 elementary school. In a mechanical room, she notices pipe insulation with a chalky, fibrous appearance typical of the era. The district's request for proposals didn't mention hazardous materials, and the district wants construction documents in four months.

Which actions are appropriate for the architect?

options.text: Notify the owner in writing of the suspected material
options.explanation: Correct. Prompt written notice lets the owner, who is responsible for testing and abatement, act.

options.text: Recommend that the owner retain an environmental consultant
options.explanation: Correct. Hazardous-material investigation is a specialist service the owner furnishes.

options.text: Collect samples during the existing-conditions survey
options.explanation: Sampling suspected asbestos exposes staff to hazards and the firm to liability. It's a specialist task.

options.text: Include removal in the general demolition scope
options.explanation: Treating suspected asbestos as routine demolition endangers workers and violates abatement rules.

options.text: Note the insulation as existing to remain
options.explanation: Leaving a known concern unaddressed falls short of reasonable care.

options.text: Have the contractor test the material during bidding
options.explanation: Testing should come from the owner's qualified consultant before documents are finalized.

questions.explanation: Suspected hazardous materials: notify the owner and recommend a specialist (B101-2017 §10.6).
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph references per my knowledge of B101-2017; confirm in your copy.

questions.stem:
A county retains an architect to design a community center on a coastal site. Current flood maps show the site just outside the regulatory flood zone, but published regional projections place it within the floodplain during the building's expected 50-year service life. The county's project manager asks for a design that meets code minimums, noting that the budget is tight.

Which response best reflects the standard of care?

options.text: Design to code minimums, since the code reflects the standard of care.
options.explanation: Codes are minimums. A reasonably foreseeable risk calls for informing the client.

options.text: Inform the county of the risk and options, and document its decision.
options.explanation: Correct. Identify the foreseeable climate risk, advise on resilience options, and record the client's informed choice (AIA 2.401, 6.501).

options.text: Require elevation of the building as a condition of the agreement.
options.explanation: The architect advises. An informed client may choose a lawful, code-compliant design.

options.text: Add resilience measures and inform the county at the end of design.
options.explanation: Adding scope and cost without the client's timely, informed decision overrides the client's authority.

questions.explanation: Climate risk: identify, advise, offer options, document. Codes are a floor.

questions.stem:
A peer reviewer checks a firm's 95% construction documents for a medical office building and reports four problems. The project architect has to classify each one in the firm's quality-control log as an error or an omission.

Which problem is best described as an omission?

options.text: The door schedule lists the wrong fire rating for a stair door.
options.explanation: Incorrect information on the documents is an error.

options.text: Two sheets show different ceiling heights for the same room.
options.explanation: Conflicting information is an error or coordination problem.

options.text: The specifications have no firestopping section.
options.explanation: Correct. Leaving out required content is an omission.

options.text: A beam is sized for the wrong span.
options.explanation: An incorrect calculation is an error.

questions.explanation: Error = shown wrong. Omission = left out.

questions.stem:
Near substantial completion, the owner's lender sends the architect a certificate to sign that states: 'Architect certifies that all work complies with the Contract Documents.' The architect made 18 site visits under the agreement and observed the work periodically.

Which revision best keeps the certificate within the standard of care?

options.text: Qualify it to knowledge and belief, based on site visits.
options.explanation: Correct. Qualified language tied to actual observation states a professional opinion, not a guarantee (B101-2017 §10.4).

options.text: Certify compliance only for the work the architect saw.
options.explanation: It's still an absolute certification, just over a smaller area.

options.text: Add that the contractor is responsible for compliance.
options.explanation: The architect's own statement would remain an unqualified certification.

options.text: Sign it as written, since the work was observed.
options.explanation: Periodic observation can't support an absolute certification of all work.

questions.explanation: Certificates: qualify the language, stay within scope, tie statements to actual observation.
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph references per my knowledge of B101-2017; confirm in your copy.

questions.stem:
During selective demolition in a 1920s commercial building, the contractor uncovers deteriorated floor framing hidden behind plaster that was in place during the architect's existing-conditions survey. The owner didn't authorize exploratory probes during design. The structural engineer estimates 40 hours to redesign the affected bays.

How should the redesign work be characterized?

options.text: As basic services, with no additional compensation
options.explanation: Concealed conditions that couldn't reasonably be found aren't a failure of the standard of care. Redesign goes beyond basic services.

options.text: As an additional service, after notifying the owner
options.explanation: Correct. Services needed because of unforeseen conditions are generally additional services (B101-2017 Art. 4).

options.text: As the contractor's design responsibility
options.explanation: Design remains the architect's responsibility.

options.text: As a claim under the architect's liability policy
options.explanation: Professional liability responds to negligence. This condition doesn't involve any.

questions.explanation: Unknown conditions → notify, document, resolve through the contract. Redesign is usually an additional service.

questions.stem:
An owner's attorney is preparing a professional negligence claim against an architect over a leaking curtain wall. An expert will testify that the architect's flashing detail fell below the standard of care, and the owner has repair invoices totaling $340,000.

Which elements must the owner generally prove to recover?

options.text: Duty, breach, causation, and damages
options.explanation: Correct. These are the four elements of negligence.

options.text: Duty, breach, intent, and damages
options.explanation: Negligence doesn't require intent.

options.text: Breach, causation, and a code violation
options.explanation: A code violation may be evidence, but duty and damages must still be shown.

options.text: Duty, an error in the documents, and damages
options.explanation: An error alone isn't a breach. It must fall below the standard of care and cause the damages.

questions.stem:
An owner's budget for a library renovation includes a construction contingency of 5% on a $4,200,000 construction cost. Midway through construction, these items have been paid from the contingency:

- Concealed structural repairs: $96,000
- Owner-requested finish upgrades: $70,000
- Premium to add an omitted fire damper, beyond its original cost: $18,000

How much contingency remains?

options.explanation: This leaves out the omitted-item premium.
This counts only the concealed structural repairs.
That's the amount spent, not the amount remaining.

questions.explanation:
1. Contingency = 5% × $4,200,000 = $210,000
2. Spent = $96,000 + $70,000 + $18,000 = $184,000
3. Remaining = $210,000 − $184,000 = $26,000
An owner's contingency is how ordinary document imperfections and unforeseen conditions get funded.

flashcards.back: The skill and care ordinarily provided by architects practicing in the same or similar locality under similar circumstances (B101-2017 §2.2).

flashcards.front: How the standard of care is proven
flashcards.back: Usually by expert testimony from other architects.

flashcards.front: Warranty words to avoid in contracts
flashcards.back: Guarantee, warrant, ensure, certify (unqualified), highest, best, all.
They raise the duty above negligence and are generally excluded from professional liability insurance.
Error = something shown or specified incorrectly. Omission = something required that was left out.
Owner pays what an omitted item would have cost originally. The architect may owe only the added cost caused by the late addition.
Budget reserve for unforeseen conditions and ordinary document imperfections. Recommend it.
Notify the owner in writing and recommend a qualified consultant. Don't sample, abate, ignore or guarantee.

flashcards.front: Who furnishes surveys, geotech and tests under B101?
flashcards.back: The owner (Article 5). The architect may rely on them.
Notify, document, evaluate, and resolve via the change process. Redesign is usually an additional service.

flashcards.front: Climate risk and the standard of care
flashcards.back: Identify foreseeable climate hazards, advise the client on resilience options beyond code minimums, and document decisions. AIA Rules 2.401 and 6.501 require informing clients of environmental impacts and considering effects with them; E.S. 6.5 covers climate adaptation.

flashcards.front: Are codes the full measure of the architect's duty?
flashcards.back: No. Codes are minimums. Reasonable care may call for advising beyond them when risks are known.
"To the best of the architect's knowledge, information and belief," within the scope of services and based on site observations.
